kidText: Quartz is a common mineral that can become silicon.
Silicon is the flat base where chip patterns are printed.
A chip starts with rocks, not with magic.
nerdText: Quartz is mostly silicon dioxide. Semiconductor manufacturing turns silicon-bearing feedstock into very pure silicon, then into crystal ingots and wafers for circuit fabrication.
realStat: Silicon is one of Earth's most abundant crustal elements, but chipmaking needs it in an extremely purified and controlled form.

lockedHint.kid: Mine quartz to unlock this entry.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the Chapter 1 quartz fact card.

kidText: Copper helps electricity move.
Chips and circuit boards both depend on good conductors.
Fast machines still need tiny metal paths.
nerdText: Copper is a key conductive material in electronics. In chip systems it appears across wiring, boards, cables, and power delivery, connecting computation to the rest of the machine.
realStat: Modern electronics supply chains track copper closely because it is used across power, interconnect, and infrastructure layers.

lockedHint.kid: Mine copper to unlock this entry.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the Chapter 1 copper fact card.

kidText: Lithium helps batteries store energy.
Data centers need backup power when the grid has trouble.
The chip journey also needs energy storage.
nerdText: Lithium is best known in this game as a battery material. It connects semiconductor supply chains to energy resilience, backup systems, and mobile devices that chips power.
realStat: Lithium-ion batteries are widely used because they store high energy for their weight compared with many older battery chemistries.

lockedHint.kid: Mine lithium to unlock this entry.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the Chapter 1 lithium fact card.

kidText: Cobalt can help some batteries work well.
Where minerals come from matters.
Supply chains connect technology to real places.
nerdText: Cobalt is a strategic mineral in parts of the battery supply chain and an example of why technology manufacturing is tied to labor, trade, environmental, and geopolitical questions.
realStat: Cobalt sourcing is often discussed alongside battery chemistry, mining conditions, and supply-chain due diligence.

lockedHint.kid: Mine cobalt to unlock this entry.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the Chapter 1 cobalt fact card.

kidText: Rare earths are a family of special elements.
They help make magnets, screens, motors, and tools.
Some tiny parts need unusual materials.
nerdText: Rare-earth elements are not always rare in the ground, but separating and refining them can be difficult. They matter across electronics, magnets, optics, and manufacturing equipment.
realStat: Rare-earth supply chains are usually discussed by separation and refining capacity, not only by what is mined.

lockedHint.kid: Mine rare earths to unlock this entry.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the Chapter 1 rare-earths fact card.

kidText: Chip silicon has to be very clean.
A tiny wrong atom can cause a tiny circuit problem.
Purity is why refining takes so much care.
nerdText: Semiconductor-grade silicon is purified far beyond ordinary industrial material. The goal is not merely cleanliness, but controlled electrical behavior with impurities introduced only where they are intended.
realStat: 9N means 99.9999999 percent purity, a shorthand used to explain extremely pure materials.

lockedHint.kid: Reach the purity lesson in Chapter 2.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the nine-nines fact card.

kidText: Factories need more than rocks.
Refining and fabs use energy and water.
Resource limits shape where technology gets made.
nerdText: Semiconductor supply chains are also energy and water systems. Power prices, water availability, treatment, reuse, and infrastructure reliability can shape where capacity is built.
realStat: Large semiconductor facilities often report water reuse, power sourcing, and efficiency because these inputs affect operations.

lockedHint.kid: Run the refinery to learn about energy and water.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the Chapter 2 energy fact card.

kidText: A seed crystal can grow a shiny silicon ingot.
Pulling steadily makes a better crystal.
The round crystal becomes round wafers.
nerdText: The Czochralski process grows a single-crystal silicon ingot by pulling a seed from molten silicon under controlled thermal and rotational conditions.
realStat: The method is named for Jan Czochralski, whose early twentieth-century work led to a major crystal-growth technique.

lockedHint.kid: Grow an ingot in Chapter 3.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the Czochralski fact card.

kidText: Wafers are round because the crystal is round.
A wafer is a thin slice from the ingot.
Tiny rectangular chips are printed on the round slice.
nerdText: Semiconductor wafers inherit their circular shape from cylindrical ingots. The circular wafer is then patterned with many rectangular dies, with edge area less usable than the center.
realStat: Mainstream silicon wafer diameters have grown over time so more dies can be processed together.

lockedHint.kid: Slice wafers in Chapter 3.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the round wafers fact card.

kidText: Fab workers wear suits to keep dust away.
Dust can be huge compared with chip features.
Cleanrooms protect the patterns.
nerdText: Cleanrooms control particles, airflow, clothing, chemicals, and procedures because nanoscale patterning can be damaged by contamination that would be invisible in ordinary rooms.
realStat: Cleanroom classifications count particles in air; chipmaking needs far tighter control than normal indoor spaces.

lockedHint.kid: Enter the fab in Chapter 4.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the cleanroom fact card.

kidText: Lithography prints tiny patterns with light.
The pattern tells the chip where circuits go.
Better alignment means better chips.
nerdText: Photolithography transfers circuit patterns onto a wafer by using light-sensitive material, masks or reticles, exposure tools, and tightly controlled alignment.
realStat: A modern chip is built from many patterned layers, not from one single print.

lockedHint.kid: Reach Chapter 4 to unlock lithography.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks when the fab chapter is available.

kidText: The tiniest patterns need very special light.
EUV machines are some of the most complex tools in factories.
One tool can shape a whole supply chain.
nerdText: EUV lithography uses extremely short-wavelength light to pattern advanced chips. The ecosystem for these tools is highly specialized and concentrated.
realStat: Public industry reporting commonly describes leading-edge EUV scanners as among the most expensive and complex manufacturing tools.

lockedHint.kid: Find the EUV fact in Chapter 4.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the EUV and ASML fact card.

kidText: Sometimes chipmakers add tiny amounts of other atoms.
Those atoms help control electricity.
The trick is adding the right amount in the right place.
nerdText: Doping deliberately introduces selected atoms into semiconductor regions to tune electrical behavior. This is different from random contamination, which can harm devices.
realStat: Semiconductor devices depend on controlled regions with different electrical properties, including doped regions.

lockedHint.kid: Reach the fab chapter to unlock doping.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks when Chapter 4 is available.

kidText: Yield means how many chips work.
Some dies on a wafer can fail tests.
Better process control makes more good chips.
nerdText: Yield is the share of manufactured dies that meet requirements. It depends on design, process maturity, defects, wafer quality, and test criteria.
realStat: Yield is central to chip economics because every wafer costs money even when some dies fail.

lockedHint.kid: Print a wafer in Chapter 4.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the defect and dust fact card.

kidText: Not every good chip is equally fast.
Testing sorts chips into bins.
A slower chip can still be useful.
nerdText: Binning sorts tested dies or packaged chips by performance, power, and defect behavior. It lets manufacturers sell usable parts at different grades instead of treating every imperfection as total waste.
realStat: Binning is common in processors, memory, and many electronic parts where tested performance varies.

lockedHint.kid: Sort dies in Chapter 5.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the binning fact card.

kidText: The CPU is a flexible leader.
It handles many kinds of instructions.
Most computers need one.
nerdText: A CPU is built for general-purpose computation and control flow. In the game it improves whole-building coordination because CPUs organize many different tasks.
realStat: CPUs appear in phones, laptops, servers, cars, appliances, and embedded systems.

lockedHint.kid: Meet the chip roster in Chapter 5.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the chip roster fact card.

kidText: The GPU has many tiny workers.
It is good at jobs that split into lots of pieces.
Graphics and AI can both use that power.
nerdText: GPUs are parallel processors designed to run many operations at once. That makes them useful for graphics, matrix math, simulation, and many AI workloads.
realStat: The AI boom has made accelerator and GPU supply a central data-center planning issue.

lockedHint.kid: Meet the chip roster in Chapter 5.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the chip roster fact card.

kidText: DRAM remembers things quickly.
It forgets when power is gone.
Fast work needs fast memory.
nerdText: DRAM is volatile working memory. It is fast enough for active computation, but it needs refresh power and loses stored data when power is removed.
realStat: Servers use large amounts of DRAM so processors can reach active data quickly.

lockedHint.kid: Meet the chip roster in Chapter 5.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the chip roster fact card.

kidText: NAND keeps data after power turns off.
It is storage, not working memory.
A vault remembers slowly but safely.
nerdText: NAND flash is non-volatile memory. It stores data in SSDs, phones, cameras, and many embedded systems even when devices are powered down.
realStat: NAND flash is a core technology behind solid-state drives and many portable devices.

lockedHint.kid: Meet the chip roster in Chapter 5.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the chip roster fact card.

kidText: The NIC helps machines talk.
A data center needs fast messages between racks.
Many computers can act like one big system.
nerdText: Network interface controllers and specialized network chips move data between machines. In data centers, fast networking is part of compute performance.
realStat: Large data centers depend on high-speed network fabrics as much as on individual processors.

lockedHint.kid: Meet the chip roster in Chapter 5.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the chip roster fact card.

kidText: The PMIC helps control power.
Chips need the right voltage at the right time.
Saving energy can save the whole system.
nerdText: Power management ICs regulate voltage, sequencing, conversion, and delivery. They make electronic systems more reliable and efficient.
realStat: Power delivery is a major design constraint from phones to servers.

lockedHint.kid: Meet the chip roster in Chapter 5.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after the chip roster fact card.

kidText: Nova is the endgame chip.
It needs a very good die.
Hard chips need the best process control.
nerdText: Nova represents specialized accelerators built for demanding AI workloads. In the game, it requires a high-quality leading-edge die because advanced nodes are harder to manufacture well.
realStat: Specialized accelerators are often designed around workload needs such as matrix math, memory bandwidth, and power limits.

lockedHint.kid: Reach the data center finale.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks when Chapter 6 is available.

kidText: A data center is more than chips.
Racks need power, cooling, and network links.
The whole building turns chips into services.
nerdText: Data centers combine servers, racks, power distribution, cooling, storage, networking, controls, and operations. Individual chips matter most when the system around them can support their work.
realStat: Data-center planning commonly tracks power capacity, cooling capacity, utilization, and network throughput together.

lockedHint.kid: Finish Chapter 6 to unlock this entry.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks after completing the data-center finale.

kidText: The chip journey crosses many steps.
Mining, refining, fabs, packaging, and data centers all connect.
Your final service depends on the whole chain.
nerdText: The complete semiconductor system links mineral extraction, chemical refining, crystal growth, wafer fabrication, packaging, test, logistics, power infrastructure, and data-center operations.
realStat: A finished chip reflects many specialized industries and international supply-chain dependencies before it reaches a working system.

lockedHint.kid: Complete the game to unlock the full map.
lockedHint.nerd: Unlocks when the Chapter 6 victory is complete.
